figures.caption: Figure 4: Graph-centric view of omission-aware reasoning. The Difference-Aware Coherence block (left) turns each coherence edge (si, sk) ∈ Ecoh into the weight κcoh(x (ℓ) a ,x (ℓ) b ) = exp(−∥Wcoh(x (ℓ) a − x (ℓ) b )∥22) of Eq. (3). The Edge-Conditioned Cross-Source Attention block (right) fuses node states with the relation embedding rij via the bilinear score of Eq. (4), yielding edge-conditioned messages. Heterograph update (center) alternates the two message types over L layers; a virtual root produces the full-news embedding g(0), which is residually merged with the propagated states into the global-narrative summary m of Eq. (6). Sentence mean pooling of the refined states {h̃i} feeds the MLP classifier that predicts Real/Fake.

Figure 1: An omission-relevant misinformation case. The target article appears locally coherent, so a detector that reasons only over what is stated is likely to label it as real. Contemporaneous reports, however, reveal that only two officers were on duty and that the protest had attempted to storm government buildings, facts the article suppresses. LCV reconstructs these omitted facts as short cross-source relations and reasons over them in a heterograph, exposing the deception that surface-level reasoning misses.

Figure 5: Qualitative LCV prediction on a selective-news-reporting case from the English dataset. Panel 1 contains the target article with three sentences {si} that are locally coherent under a presentedonly view. Panel 2 lists the retrieved context articles {cj} that supply the omitted background, causal trigger, and outcome. Panel 3 visualizes the reconstructed missing-context relations zij as dark sentence–article edges in the heterograph G, with light edges denoting intra-target coherence in Ecoh. Panel 4 shows the same bipartite structure consumed by the omission-aware reasoner of Section 3.4: the compact prediction head moves from a weak Real decision under the presented-only view to a confident Fake decision once the recovered relations are integrated, with the bottom strip attributing the shift to missing background, missing causality, and missing consequence.

Table 3: Main comparison on the English and Chinese datasets. Higher is better. Re-run baselines and LCV are reported as mean±standard deviation over three runs. Entries marked with † are taken from the published paper and therefore do not include re-run variance. ∗ indicates that the improvement of LCV over OmiGraph is statistically significant at the 0.005 level under a paired t-test.

Figure 2: Overview of LCV. (a) Retrieval-guided graph construction selects the top-K temporally aligned context articles from the candidate pool C(P ) within a ∆-day look-back window via TF–IDF cosine similarity, and assembles a heterograph over target sentence nodes Vs and context article nodes Vc. (b) For each sentence–article pair (si, cj) ∈ Esc, a frozen LLM qϕ reconstructs a short missing-context description zij , which is encoded by the shared text encoder and projected into the cross-source relation embedding rij . (c) Omission-aware graph reasoning propagates messages along three edge types, namely intra-target coherence edges Ecoh, s→c and c→s cross-source edges with rij as edge features, and combines them with a closed-form document-level summary m before a binary classifier predicts y ∈ {real,misinfo}.

Figure 3: Construction of textual cross-source relations. For each sentence–article pair (si, cj), a frozen LLM qϕ is queried with a fixed prompt template that asks it to output one short phrase summarizing a fact present in cj but absent from si, or the sentinel [NO_MISSING_CONTEXT] when no such fact exists. Generated phrases zij are encoded by the shared BERT backbone ftext and projected by Πr into the cross-source relation embedding rij ∈ Rd, while [NO_MISSING_CONTEXT] outputs are mapped to a learnable null embedding r∅. The resulting embeddings are attached as edge features to the heterograph used in Figure 2(c).
